title: Five hallelujahs (Psalms 146–150)
hookLine: the last five psalms, each beginning and ending with praise
last: THE LORD UPHOLDETH ALL THAT FALL.

cards: Hallelujah. It rings out in gospel choirs and in Handel's Messiah, turns up on greeting cards, and gets muttered when the bus finally comes. Said that way, it can sound like a sigh of relief.

In Hebrew it's two words joined, and it's an instruction. In the Jewish morning service, right after Ashrei, it comes again and again, like bookends, at the start and end of each of the last five psalms in the Bible.

teach.h: HALLELU-YAH: ALL OF YOU, PRAISE GOD.
teach.b: Hallelu means praise, said to a group: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's name. So hallelujah is a call: everyone, praise God.
Psalms one hundred forty-six through one hundred fifty each open and close with it: five psalms, ten hallelujahs. Listen to the praise widen.

teach.h: THE PRISONER, THE STRANGER, THE WIDOW.
teach.b: The first praises God for the people at the bottom: the prisoner, the blind, the stranger, the orphan, the widow.
The second, in the old Jewish translation, says God is the one "Who healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds," and in the same breath counts the stars and calls each by name.
The third calls on everything to praise: sun and moon, sea creatures, fire and hail, kings and children, old and young. The fourth asks for a new song.
And the last is almost all music: horn, harp, drum, dancing, strings, pipes, cymbals, loud cymbals.
Then the final line of the whole Book of Psalms: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Hallelujah."
The prayer book says that line twice. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records Rabbi Yose's wish to be among those who finish the praise every day, understood to mean these psalms.
So the Book of Psalms, with all its grief and pleading, ends here: not with an answer, but with everything that breathes, praising.

how: Psalms 146–150 are said every morning in the verses of song, right after Ashrei, with the last verse of Psalm 150 repeated; in many synagogues they are chanted quickly together, and the final verses are sung aloud.

games.q: the Book of Psalms holds grief, anger, pleading and joy. how does it end?
games.why: let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. hallelujah. the prayer book says the line twice.

practice: If you have a Bible or prayer book nearby, open to Psalm one hundred fifty, only six verses, and read it slowly, aloud if you can; if not, stay with its last line, let every thing that hath breath.
Breathe in, notice your own breath, and think of three other things that breathe near you: a person, a pet, a tree outside. If you pray, end with hallelujah.
